body.text: A few days ago I spent some an hour on the phone with a friend in Gaza. Before the war, our conversations were a kind of luxury. He was a director-general in one of the Palestinian Authority’s ministries, educated in the United States and the Netherlands, from a family whose name carries weight in Gaza going back generations. We talked about political theories, we discussed Francis Fukuyama’s The End of History, Naomi Klein’s The Shock Doctrine. We argued about language, about what words do and fail to do. He had opinions about world politics that were sharper than most of what I now hear in rooms packed by political advisers, and he enjoyed being right about them.
This time, about ten minutes in, he said: “Our horizon of function is twenty-four hours.”

He did not say it dramatically. He said it the way an engineer tells you the load-bearing limit of a beam. Then he explained what that horizon contains. Where the water will come from today. How many hours of the day are spent getting it. Where bread might be found, and at what hour the line stops being worth standing in. And then, in the same register, without raising his voice: a few days earlier, an airstrike had hit a car a few metres from where his family is staying. His boys saw it.
He moved on quickly. I did not.
Because I had just come from rooms in which he did not exist.

On the margins of the UN high-level week, I sat with foreign ministers from the Middle East and Europe, officials from the Board of Peace, senior figures from the UN system. The discussions were serious; the people in them were not cynical.

The agenda was regional: Yemen, Iran, Iraq, Lebanon, Palestine. Five files, each of which could absorb a career, and the people at the table had the standing to discuss all five. At some point I noticed the discussion was back, naturally, to focus on Palestine especially Gaza, continuously, with care, and not one individual human being from Gaza entered the conversation. Not as an absence of sympathy. As an absence of texture.

My friend has a PhD and three decades of administrative experience. He is precisely the person those rooms claim to be planning for. In the language of the room, he is an affected population. He is a displaced person.

The paradox is that Gaza may be the most documented place on earth; photographed from satellites and from phones, filmed by drones and by teenagers, mapped by militaries and by aid agencies, counted, tabulated, disputed, invoked in parliaments and at dinner tables in cities where no one has ever heard a military drone or a warplane fweep in the middle of the night. There has never been a shortage of images.
And somewhere inside all that visibility, the person disappears.
What does it mean to become invisible while the whole world is watching you?

It begins with categories. To be discussed at scale, people must be sorted. So they become the displaced. They become casualties, civilians, aid recipients, the population of Gaza, people in humanitarian need. These are not malicious words. They are necessary ones; you cannot run a corridor or negotiate a crossing without them. But a category is a container, and what it holds is not the same shape as its contents.

Because someone was a teacher. Someone was insufferable about his coffee and would not drink it any other way. Someone was worried about her daughter’s grades, specifically in mathematics, specifically because the girl was bright but lazy. Someone had nearly saved enough to marry. Someone was in a long, petty, deeply committed feud with his neighbour over a fence. Someone was finally renovating his house. Someone was applying to university. Someone paid for a gym but never stepped a foot in. Someone was in love and had said nothing. Someone was simply bored, bored in the ordinary, unbearable, entirely human way that has nothing to do with Palestine or Israel or Hamas or war at all.
Then the world came to know them by their humanitarian classification.

This is the second destruction, and nobody photographs it. The first destruction is physical: the house, the street, the bakery, the route you took to work without thinking. The second is the disappearance of the individual from the way the world speaks about what happened to the individual. The first is done with ordnance. The second is done with vocabulary, and with our own attention, and it happens quietly, and it happens to people who are still alive.

I want to be careful here, because there is a way of writing about Gaza that claims to correct this and instead deepens it, the essay that presents Palestinians as an undifferentiated mass of suffering bodies, tender, passive, and finally just as anonymous as the statistics it set out to humanise. Suffering alone does not make a person visible. It can be the very thing that hides them.
So let me stay inside the twenty-four hours, because that is where the actual person lives.

Is there enough water to drink, or should some be kept for washing. Is this road safer than that road, and safer by how much, and does that margin justify the twenty minutes it saves. How many hours in the bread line before the waiting costs more than the bread is worth. Should a parent leave three children in a damaged room in order to find food for them. Is that crack in the wall the kind that waits or the kind that doesn’t. If the displacement order comes tonight, what can actually be carried, the documents, yes, and the blanket, and the pot, but not the photo album, because the pot cooks and the photographs do not. Where will an elderly father sleep, given that he can no longer sleep on the ground. How does a mother decide which child gets the last of something, knowing the other one is watching her decide. How do you charge a phone when the phone is the only route to your brother, to news, to aid registration, to knowing whether the people you love are alive.

And underneath all of it, the thing that makes this unlike hardship anywhere else: several of these ordinary decisions carry the possibility of death. Going for water is a decision. Looking for bread is a decision. Choosing one street over another is a decision. Staying is a decision, and leaving is a decision, and nothing on the list is simply neutral. My friend’s sons did not go anywhere unusual. The car came to them.
In most societies these are only reflexes, performed below the level of thought. In Gaza they are conducted with the full attention of an adult mind, dozens of times a day, for years.
Which brings me to the question I am asked most often by people who mean well. Why don’t Gazans protest more? What do they really think of Hamas? What political future do they actually want?

These are legitimate questions, and Gazans have sharp, unsentimental, frequently furious answers to all of them. I have never met a population less romantic about its own rulers. But the questions miss something structural. Survival conquers attention. It does not extinguish political thought; it occupies the territory where political thought is supposed to live, the way an army occupies a city.

Consider what this means in my friend’s case. Here is a man trained in exactly the disciplines those conference rooms require, fluent in their languages, experienced in their procedures, with views on governance formed over thirty years of practice. He is not politically passive. He is one of the most politically literate people I know. And his capacity has been requisitioned, not by ideology, but by water.
We are asking people under siege to produce position papers.

And here is what disturbs me most, because it implicates the very technology we assumed would prevent it. We are living through one of the most densely documented catastrophe in modern history. People in Gaza film themselves queueing, cooking beside tents, digging, burying, walking through what used to be their neighborhoods. They are not asking to be pitied. They are asking to be entered into the record as having existed in a particular way.

But documentation is not recognition. A face can cross ten million screens in an afternoon and arrive nowhere. We have built an infrastructure that delivers images at a volume the moral imagination was never designed to absorb, and the imagination does what any overloaded system does: it compresses. The footage keeps coming, and the person inside it gets thinner.

Perhaps the tragedy is not that Gaza went unseen. Gaza is seen constantly, relentlessly, from every angle and by every instrument we possess. The tragedy is that after looking at Gaza for so long, we may have lost the ability to see anyone in it.

I do not have a political solution to offer, and I am suspicious of essays that end by producing one. What I want is smaller and harder. Before the next round of arguments, about who is right, who is responsible, what should be sequenced, what should be conditioned, I want to ask whether we can still perform the older act that all those arguments are supposed to serve.

Can we see them not as Palestinians, victims, supporters, opponents, refugees, statistics or symbols, but as individuals: mundane, contradictory, privately ambitious, quietly anxious, occasionally petty, in love, in debt, in the middle of something?

My friend was not mentioned in that room. He would have understood every word spoken in it. He has a name, a family, a profession, a library, and a set of opinions I used to enjoy losing arguments to. Today he has a horizon of twenty-four hours, and inside it, water, bread and two boys who saw a car explode a few metres from where they sleep. He does not need pity, and he has not asked for opinions.

He needs what every person is owed and what no ceasefire delivers on its own: to be known as someone rather than as something. The measure of our seriousness is not how much of Gaza we have seen. It is whether, after all of it, we can still see a single human being. •
